segments.text: [style: brisk, clear, architectural voice; steady studio cadence] Book Three, Proposition Twenty-One. In a circle, angles in the same segment are equal to one another. Let A B C D be a circle, and let angles B A D and B E D lie in the same circle segment B A E D. We are to prove that angle B A D equals angle B E D.

segments.text: [style: luminous, deductive geometric clarity] Because angle B F D is at the center and angle B A D is at the circumference, and both stand on the same base arc B C D, by Three Twenty angle B F D is double angle B A D. For the exact same reason, angle B F D is also double angle B E D. Since both inscribed angles are halves of the same central angle B F D, angle B A D equals angle B E D, as was required to prove.

segments.text: [style: reflective, scholarly, architectural synthesis] As Heath notes, Euclid's direct appeal to Three Twenty assumes a segment greater than a semicircle so the central angle B F D is less than two right angles; Robert Simson extended the proof to all segments by drawing diameter A F C to split the angle into two major segments. Its converse establishes the fundamental test for concyclic points: any vertices on the same side of a base that subtend equal angles lie on one circle. In the GEOMETOR G-Index, node G one hundred twenty-four synthesizes six direct rules across fifty ancestor nodes, turning the central-angle ratio of Three Twenty into a direct invariant of the circumference.
